title: Field Extension
body:
A [[Field]] $K$ containing a field $F$ as a subfield, written $K/F$. You build one when $F$ is
missing a root you want, and the construction is always the same: **take a polynomial with no
root in $F$, and quotient by it.**

$$K = F[x]/(f), \qquad f \text{ irreducible over } F$$

By [[Irreducibility]] that quotient is a field, and inside it the class $[x]$ satisfies
$f([x]) = 0$. The root you wanted now exists, because you built the smallest structure in which
it has to.

## The worked example is $\mathbb{C}$

$x^2 + 1$ has no root in $\mathbb{R}$. So

$$\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2+1)$$

Elements are remainders on division by a degree-2 polynomial, so they all look like $a + bx$;
write $i$ for the class of $x$ and the relation $x^2 \equiv -1$ becomes $i^2 = -1$. Multiplication
is polynomial multiplication followed by reduction:

```
(a + bi)(c + di) = ac + (ad + bc)i + bd·i²
                 = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i     using i² = -1
```

which is exactly the arithmetic [[Complex Numbers]] states in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]. Nothing is
imagined or postulated; $i$ is a coset, and the rule $i^2 = -1$ is what reducing mod $x^2+1$ does.
**This is the middle rung of the vault's complex-numbers ladder**: MATH 1203 takes $\mathbb{C}$ as
arithmetic and geometry, this course as structure, and [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] as
analysis.

## Degree

$K$ is a [[Vector Space]] over $F$, and its dimension is the **degree** of the extension,
$[K:F]$. If $K = F[x]/(f)$ then $\{1, \alpha, \alpha^2, \dots, \alpha^{n-1}\}$ is a [[Basis]],
where $n = \deg f$ and $\alpha$ is the adjoined root, so

$$[K:F] = \deg f$$

$[\mathbb{C}:\mathbb{R}] = 2$, with basis $\{1, i\}$, which is the precise sense in which a
complex number is a two-dimensional real object. $[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2):\mathbb{Q}] = 2$ with basis
$\{1,\sqrt2\}$, so $a + b\sqrt2$ is the general element and rationalising a denominator is
computing an inverse in that field.

Degrees multiply through a tower: $[M:F] = [M:K][K:F]$. That single fact kills the classical
construction problems, since a straightedge-and-compass step only ever gives degree 2, so every
constructible number has degree a power of 2, and doubling the cube needs degree 3.

## Algebraic and transcendental

$\alpha$ is **algebraic** over $F$ if it is a root of some non-zero polynomial with coefficients
in $F$, and **transcendental** otherwise. $\sqrt2$ and $i$ are algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$;
$\pi$ and $e$ are not, which is the other reason squaring the circle is impossible. An extension
generated by one algebraic element is finite, with degree equal to the degree of that element's
minimal polynomial.

## Where the course goes next

Adjoining roots to $\mathbb{Z}_p$ instead of $\mathbb{R}$ is how every [[Finite Field]] beyond the
prime ones is built, and it is why their sizes are exactly the prime powers $p^n$: $n$ is the
degree of the extension, and a vector space of dimension $n$ over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ has $p^n$
elements. Counting the field is counting coordinate tuples.
